research_questions.RQ1: Which detector has the highest recall on unseen attack families at a fixed false-alarm budget?
research_questions.RQ2: Does score fusion improve worst-case family recall?
research_questions.RQ3: How much does each method degrade across datasets?
research_questions.RQ4: Is it better to model normal traffic, or known attacks with an unknown-rejection rule?

zero_day_proxy: Hold out entire attack families from training, tuning, and threshold selection; evaluate them only in the final test split. This is a zero-day-style benchmark proxy and does not establish real zero-day detection.

tuning.model_settings: fixed a priori; no attack-family labels are used for fitting, feature preprocessing, fusion weighting, or threshold selection
tuning.held_out_families: all six observed non-benign families are evaluated one at a time

thresholding.quantile_rule: threshold at empirical benign calibration score quantile 1 - target_fpr; score >= threshold is anomalous

datasets.primary: CICIDS2017 Cleaned & Preprocessed (Kaggle dataset by ericanacletoribe; cleaning provenance and licence pending audit)
datasets.cross_dataset: CSE-CIC-IDS2018 or BCCC-CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (pending column compatibility audit)

limitations: Held-out attack families are a benchmark proxy, not real zero-day attacks.
Public benchmark datasets may be old, simulated, and limited to a single testbed.
An anomaly score is not an attack probability, and an alert is not proof of an attack.
Performance on one dataset does not establish performance on independent real-world networks.
